b: The proposed Forest Bioeconomy Act would expand US Forest Service research partnerships and encourage commercial uses of underused timber, including in mass timber construction.
Greater commercial use of low-value timber could support forest management and create new opportunities for the US wood products industry (Image: Unsplash)
US lawmakers have put forward bipartisan legislation to strengthen the US forest products industry by creating new commercial opportunities for low-value timber.

Representatives Glenn “GT” Thompson (Republican-Pennsylvania) and Kim Schrier (Democrat-Washington) introduced the Forest Bioeconomy Act on 18 Nov 2026. The legislation seeks to stimulate demand for underused timber by encouraging its use in wood products, including mass timber, while supporting sustainable forest management and affordable housing.

A companion bill was introduced in the Senate by Senators Steve Daines (Republican-Montana), Raphael Warnock (Democrat-Georgia), Jim Justice (Republican-West Virginia) and Martin Heinrich (Democrat-New Mexico).

The proposed legislation would expand public-private research partnerships through the US Forest Service to accelerate the development and commercialisation of forest products. It also aims to improve the transfer of research and technologies developed in federal laboratories to manufacturers, timber businesses and landowners.
“These commonsense provisions will keep Pennsylvania’s forestry industry going for years to come, and ensure businesses have the tools necessary to meet increasing demand,” Thompson said.

According to Thompson, many forests across the US are overstocked with small-diameter, diseased, low-strength and otherwise low-value timber. This increases wildfire risks and hinders the development of healthy forest ecosystems. Creating new markets for these materials could help support forest management efforts while providing additional opportunities for timber-producing communities.

“Communities across Washington state are still reeling from the damage of last summer’s devastating wildfires,” Schrier said. “Our families also face skyrocketing prices across the board, and need relief now.”

The American Wood Council (AWC) welcomed the legislation, highlighting its potential to stimulate emerging markets such as mass timber and strengthen collaboration between the Forest Service and industry.

“Healthy forests depend on healthy markets, and right now, the wood products industry is facing real challenges,” said Jackson Morrill, president and CEO of AWC. “Homebuilder sentiment is at its lowest level in over a decade, and we are grappling with a changing residuals market.”

The Rural Voices for Conservation Coalition also endorsed the bill, saying it could help translate publicly funded research into commercially viable products and create new opportunities for rural businesses and workers.
“Forest-dependent communities have long called for investments that connect healthy forests with strong local economies,” said Cole Jenson, acting coalition director of the organisation.
Other organisations endorsing the legislation include the National Association of Forest Owners, Alliance for Wildfire Resilience and National Association of State Foresters.

Thompson’s office cited the Department of Energy (DOE) as an example of the potential benefits of stronger research and industry collaboration. The DOE has more than 40,000 patents and 1,400 active licences, compared with 42 patents and eight active licences held by the Forest Service.
